front_blocks.md: Define **enthalpy change**.

back_blocks.md: An **enthalpy change** (symbol: Δ*H*) is the heat energy transferred between a chemical system and its surroundings during a reaction at constant pressure. It can be positive (endothermic) or negative (exothermic).

cards.front_md: Define **enthalpy change**.
cards.back_md: An **enthalpy change** (symbol: Δ*H*) is the heat energy transferred between a chemical system and its surroundings during a reaction at constant pressure. It can be positive (endothermic) or negative (exothermic).

front_blocks.md: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to the temperature of the surroundings and what is the sign of ΔH?

back_blocks.md: The temperature of the surroundings **increases** because heat is **released** to the surroundings. ΔH is **negative**, as the products have less energy than the reactants.

cards.front_md: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to the temperature of the surroundings and what is the sign of ΔH?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In an endothermic reaction, ΔH is positive.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
In an endothermic reaction, heat is absorbed from the surroundings. The products have more energy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive.

front_blocks.md: In an exothermic reaction, the temperature of the **..........**  increases, while the temperature of the **..........**  decreases. ΔH is **..........** .

back_blocks.md: In an exothermic reaction, the temperature of the **surroundings** increases, while the temperature of the **system** decreases. ΔH is **negative**.

front_blocks.md: Define **exothermic reaction**.

back_blocks.md: An **exothermic reaction** is one in which energy is released to the surroundings as heat. The products have less enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is negative and the temperature of the surroundings rises.

cards.front_md: Define **exothermic reaction**.
cards.back_md: An **exothermic reaction** is one in which energy is released to the surroundings as heat. The products have less enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is negative and the temperature of the surroundings rises.

front_blocks.md: Why must the physical states of all species be specified when writing an enthalpy equation?

back_blocks.md: Changes of state involve **large enthalpy changes**. For example, dissolving NaCl (s) has ΔH = **+4 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>, but dissociating NaCl (g) has ΔH = **+500 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>. Omitting states makes the value ambiguous.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An exothermic reaction is always fast enough to observe in practice.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
An exothermic reaction is thermodynamically favourable, but the rate may be too slow to observe if the activation energy is high. In that case, the reaction is kinetically controlled.

front_blocks.md: Define **endothermic reaction**.

back_blocks.md: An **endothermic reaction** is one in which energy is absorbed from the surroundings as heat. The products have more enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive and the temperature of the surroundings falls.

cards.front_md: Define **endothermic reaction**.
cards.back_md: An **endothermic reaction** is one in which energy is absorbed from the surroundings as heat. The products have more enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive and the temperature of the surroundings falls.

front_blocks.md: Define **activation energy**.

back_blocks.md: **Activation energy** (*E*<sub>a</sub>) is the minimum amount of energy needed for reactant molecules to have a successful collision and start the reaction. It is the energy difference between the reactants and the transition state.

cards.front_md: Define **activation energy**.
cards.back_md: **Activation energy** (*E*<sub>a</sub>) is the minimum amount of energy needed for reactant molecules to have a successful collision and start the reaction. It is the energy difference between the reactants and the transition state.

front_blocks.md: On a reaction pathway diagram, what does the transition state represent and why can it not be isolated?

back_blocks.md: The transition state is a **short-lived**, **high-energy** arrangement in which bonds are **partially broken and partially formed**. It is the highest point on the energy curve and is too unstable to isolate.

In an exothermic reaction, the products are higher in energy than the reactants.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In an exothermic reaction, the products are lower in energy than the reactants. ΔH is negative and heat is released to the surroundings.

front_blocks.md: On a reaction pathway diagram, the **..........**  change (ΔH) is the energy difference between **..........**  and **..........**  . The activation energy is the energy difference from reactants to the **..........** .

back_blocks.md: On a reaction pathway diagram, the **enthalpy** change (ΔH) is the energy difference between **reactants** and **products**. The activation energy is the energy difference from reactants to the **transition state**.

front_blocks.md: Define **transition state**.

back_blocks.md: A **transition state** is the highest-energy arrangement of atoms during a reaction, where bonds are partially broken and partially formed. It is unstable and cannot be isolated.

front_blocks.md: How do you determine the activation energy of the reverse reaction from a reaction pathway diagram?

back_blocks.md: The *E*<sub>a</sub> of the **reverse reaction** is the energy difference from the energy level of the products to the top of the hump (**transition state**), measured in the reverse direction.

cards.front_md: How do you determine the activation energy of the reverse reaction from a reaction pathway diagram?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Endothermic reactions generally have a higher activation energy than exothermic reactions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Activation energy is independent of whether a reaction is endothermic or exothermic — it is determined by the energy of the **transition state** relative to the reactants. An endothermic reaction simply has products at **higher energy** than the reactants; this does not necessarily mean a higher activation energy.

back_blocks.md: The y-axis should be labelled **energy** (or enthalpy) and the x-axis should be labelled **reaction coordinate** (or extent of reaction / progress of reaction).

front_blocks.md: Define **standard enthalpy change of combustion**.

back_blocks.md: A **standard enthalpy change of combustion** (Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>) is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance in its standard state is burnt completely in excess oxygen under standard conditions. It is always exothermic.

cards.front_md: Define **standard enthalpy change of combustion**.
cards.back_md: A **standard enthalpy change of combustion** (Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>) is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance in its standard state is burnt completely in excess oxygen under standard conditions. It is always exothermic.

front_blocks.md: What are the standard conditions used for enthalpy measurements?

back_blocks.md: Standard conditions are a pressure of **101 kPa** and a temperature of **298 K (25 °C)**, with each substance in its normal physical state.

cards.front_md: What are the standard conditions used for enthalpy measurements?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The standard enthalpy change of formation of an element in its standard state is zero.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
By definition, elements in their standard state are the reference point. No reaction is needed to form them, so Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 0 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

The standard enthalpy change of formation can be either exothermic or endothermic.

front_blocks.md: Define **average bond energy**.

back_blocks.md: An **average bond energy** is the average amount of energy required to break one mole of a particular type of covalent bond across a range of different molecules. It differs from exact bond dissociation energy because bond strength is affected by the surrounding atoms.

front_blocks.md: What is the formula used to calculate heat transferred in a calorimetry experiment?

back_blocks.md: ***q******* = *******m******* x *******c******* x Δ*******T***, where *m* = mass of water (g), *c* = specific heat capacity (J g<sup>-1</sup> °C<sup>-1</sup>) and Δ*T* = temperature change (°C or K).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Bond breaking is exothermic and bond forming is endothermic.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Bond breaking is endothermic (energy is absorbed to overcome attractive forces). Bond forming is exothermic (energy is released to the surroundings).

back_blocks.md: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>r</sub> = enthalpy change for bonds **broken** + enthalpy change for bonds **formed**. Values for bond breaking are **positive** and values for bond forming are **negative**.

front_blocks.md: Define **specific heat capacity**.

back_blocks.md: **Specific heat capacity** (*c*) is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. For water, *c* = 4.18 J g<sup>-1</sup> °C<sup>-1</sup>.

back_blocks.md: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>r</sub> = +2253 + (-2346) = **-93 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>. The negative value confirms the reaction is exothermic.

front_blocks.md: Why are average bond energies used instead of exact bond dissociation energies for most enthalpy calculations?

back_blocks.md: Bond strength is affected by the **surrounding atoms** in a molecule. **Average bond energies** account for this variation by averaging the energy across many different molecular environments for the same bond type.
